# Lemuri

> Lemuri is a free, open source (MIT) desktop SSH console for the servers and VPS you manage: a tree of hosts, tabs and split terminals, uploads and downloads over SFTP from the terminal, live metrics, an encrypted password vault, one-file backups and end-to-end encrypted sharing of hosts with a team. It is native, written in C++ with Qt 6, and runs on Linux (developed and tested on Ubuntu with GNOME); macOS builds from source but is not tested on a real Mac yet.

On Ubuntu 24.04, 26.04 and 26.10 it installs from the PPA, and apt keeps it up to date:

```
sudo add-apt-repository ppa:al-redai/lemuri
sudo apt install lemuri
```

For Debian and other Ubuntu releases, a .deb package is attached to every release on GitHub (https://github.com/getlemuri/lemuri/releases/latest), with a .tar.gz for other distributions. Install it with:

```
sudo apt install ./lemuri_*_amd64.deb
```

The .deb offers and installs its updates from the app; every package is signed and checked before installing. To build from source (Qt 6.4+, libvterm, libssh, libargon2, OpenSSL, CMake, Ninja):

```
git clone https://github.com/getlemuri/lemuri
cd lemuri
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja && cmake --build build
build/lemuri
```

## Main features

- Host tree: nested folders you drag around, a mark showing which servers answer on their SSH port, a badge with the open sessions. Double-click opens the shell.
- Tabs and split panes: each terminal has a band on top (host, the shell's title, gauge and commands), one tab per session, split a terminal side by side or one above the other, on the same host or another; sync sends what you type to every pane.
- Files: drag files or folders onto a terminal to upload them to the shell's current folder (when the shell announces it with OSC 7, or with interactive mode on; otherwise the home folder); after `ls`, right-click a name to download it. Overwrites are shown before anything moves; files are written under a temporary name until complete; symbolic links are not followed.
- Files view: a folder icon in the band over a server terminal swaps the shell for two panes, this computer on the left and the server on the right (starting in the shell's folder); double-click or drag to copy across; new folder, rename and delete on both sides (local files go to the trash).
- Launch groups: named lists of servers opened together, split in one tab (two side by side, three with one large, four as a grid; more in more tabs). A folder's servers open the same way with "Open all, split". The clock button and Ctrl+Shift+O list the last five servers started.
- Live metrics: CPU, memory, disks, uptime, pending updates (and how many are security fixes) and whether a reboot is required, read over SSH with no agent on the server.
- Ghost mode: the window becomes a see-through terminal on the desktop, anchored to a screen edge; F11 hides and shows it. The files view and the Team page work there too.
- Backup: one encrypted file with hosts, vault and selected SSH keys; importing never overwrites `~/.ssh`.
- Import of `~/.ssh/config`, `ProxyJump` and keys included.
- Jump hosts like `ssh -J`; every host key at every hop is checked against `known_hosts`, new ones confirmed by hand.
- Clickable terminal (interactive mode, off by default): after `ls`, double-click a folder to enter it or a text file to open it in `nano`.
- Encrypted vault: passwords encrypted with AES-GCM under a key derived from the master password with Argon2id; key passphrases are never saved.
- Local shell tab next to the servers.
- Data in `~/.lemuri`, in the same format as the first version of Lemuri.
- Team sharing: send a host with its credentials to a teammate, sealed for them and signed by you, with no server or account. Keys are exchanged once (fingerprint compared by voice, or a 6-digit code on the same network). On a local network hosts go directly between PCs (UDP 47820 for discovery on private addresses, TCP 47821); otherwise as an encrypted text sent by email or chat.
